data.title: Acne vulgaris — viva
data.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acne vulgaris** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. Define acne vulgaris.**
- Chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit with comedones, papules, pustules, nodules and cysts on face, chest and back; affects >85% of adolescents; may persist into adulthood (adult female acne)

**Q2. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Four key factors: (1) increased sebum production under androgen control (DHT via 5α-reductase type 1 in sebocytes; IGF-1, insulin); (2) follicular hyperkeratinisation of the infundibulum → microcomedone (IL-1α, altered linoleic acid); (3) Cutibacterium acnes (phylotype IA1 dysbiosis) — activates TLR2, inflammasome (IL-1β), lipases produce free fatty acids, biofilm; (4) inflammation — may precede comedone formation (innate immunity, Th17)
- Exposome: high glycaemic-load diet, dairy (skimmed milk), whey protein, stress, cosmetics, occlusion/friction, smoking, pollution, sleep deprivation

**Q3. Grade acne (Indian/IAA grading).**
- Grade 1: comedones, occasional papules
- Grade 2: papules, comedones, few pustules
- Grade 3: predominant pustules, nodules, abscesses
- Grade 4: mainly cysts, abscesses, widespread scarring (nodulocystic/conglobata)
- Others: Global Acne Grading System (GAGS), Leeds technique, IGA; mild/moderate/severe by lesion counts

**Q4. Discuss the variants of acne (PYQ).**
- Neonatal (maternal androgens; also neonatal cephalic pustulosis — Malassezia) and infantile acne (3–6 months; persistent — check hyperandrogenism)
- Acne conglobata (nodules, abscesses, interconnecting sinuses, double comedones — men, trunk)
- Acne fulminans (sudden severe ulcerative acne with fever, arthralgia, osteolytic bone lesions, leucocytosis — adolescent boys, sometimes triggered by isotretinoin) — treat with oral steroids then low-dose isotretinoin
- Acne excoriée, acne mechanica (friction — helmets, backpacks), acne cosmetica, pomade acne, occupational (oil acne, chloracne), drug-induced/acneiform (steroids, androgens, lithium, isoniazid, phenytoin, EGFR inhibitors, halogens), tropical acne, acne aestivalis (Mallorca acne), adult female acne (lower face/jawline, hormonal), acne with facial oedema (solid facial oedema/Morbihan), gram-negative folliculitis, SAPHO and PAPA/PASH syndromes

**Q5. Discuss systemic associations of acne (PYQ).**
- Hyperandrogenism: PCOS (acne + hirsutism + irregular cycles + AN), congenital adrenal hyperplasia (late-onset 21-hydroxylase), androgen-secreting tumours (sudden virilisation), Cushing's, HAIR-AN
- Syndromes: SAPHO (Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, Osteitis), PAPA (Pyogenic Arthritis, Pyoderma gangrenosum, Acne — PSTPIP1), PASH/PAPASH (with hidradenitis), Apert syndrome (FGFR2 — severe acne), XYY, Behçet's (acneiform)
- Insulin resistance/obesity, eating disorders (bulimia — acne excoriée?), endocrine — acromegaly

**Q6. Which investigations are needed?**
- Usually none
- Hormonal work-up for women with signs of hyperandrogenism (irregular menses, hirsutism, sudden onset/resistant acne, androgenic alopecia): total/free testosterone, DHEAS, LH/FSH ratio, 17-OH progesterone, prolactin, fasting glucose/insulin, pelvic ultrasound — ideally day 2–5 of cycle
- Before isotretinoin: fasting lipids, LFT, CBC, pregnancy test (women)

**Q7. Topical treatment of acne.**
- Retinoids (tretinoin 0.025–0.1%, adapalene 0.1–0.3%, tazarotene, trifarotene 0.005% — RAR-γ selective) — comedolytic, anti-inflammatory; first-line in all grades and for maintenance
- Benzoyl peroxide 2.5–5% — bactericidal, no resistance; combine with antibiotics to prevent resistance
- Topical antibiotics (clindamycin 1%, nadifloxacin, minocycline foam 4%) — never as monotherapy
- Azelaic acid 15–20% (also for PIH), dapsone gel 5–7.5%, clascoterone 1% (topical androgen receptor antagonist), salicylic acid, niacinamide
- Fixed combinations: adapalene–BPO, clindamycin–BPO, clindamycin–tretinoin

**Q8. Discuss the various drugs used for acne (systemic) (PYQ).**
- Oral antibiotics for moderate–severe inflammatory acne: doxycycline 100 mg/day, minocycline 50–100 mg, sarecycline (narrow-spectrum), azithromycin (pulse; pregnancy alternatives erythromycin), — limit to 3–4 months, always with topical retinoid/BPO
- Hormonal (women): combined oral contraceptives (ethinyl oestradiol + drospirenone/cyproterone acetate/desogestrel), spironolactone 50–100 mg/day, cyproterone acetate, flutamide (hepatotoxicity — rarely), metformin for insulin resistance
- Oral isotretinoin: severe nodulocystic acne, scarring, treatment-resistant moderate acne, acne with psychological distress, gram-negative folliculitis; 0.25–0.5 (up to 1) mg/kg/day; cumulative 120–150 mg/kg or low-dose long-term regimens
- Others: oral zinc, dapsone (acne conglobata), oral steroids (acne fulminans, flares with isotretinoin), ibuprofen

**Q9. Isotretinoin: mechanism, side effects and monitoring.**
- Mechanism: 13-cis-retinoic acid — shrinks sebaceous glands (~90% sebum reduction), normalises follicular keratinisation, reduces C. acnes indirectly, anti-inflammatory; only drug affecting all 4 pathogenic factors
- Mucocutaneous: cheilitis (universal — compliance marker), xerosis, xerophthalmia, epistaxis, photosensitivity, retinoid dermatitis, paronychia, pyogenic granulomas, telogen effluvium
- Systemic: hypertriglyceridaemia, raised transaminases, myalgia/raised CK, headache, benign intracranial hypertension (avoid tetracyclines together), night-blindness, mood changes/depression (monitor), IBD (unproven), DISH/premature epiphyseal closure (high dose)
- Teratogenicity: craniofacial, cardiac, thymic, CNS defects — two reliable contraception methods 1 month before, during and 1 month after; monthly pregnancy test (iPLEDGE-style)
- Monitoring: lipids and LFT at baseline and 1–2 months, then as needed; mood assessment

**Q10. Discuss management of acne scars (PYQ).**
- Classification: atrophic — ice-pick (narrow deep <2 mm), boxcar (round/oval sharp walls 1.5–4 mm), rolling (wide undulating); hypertrophic and keloidal scars (chest, back, jawline); Goodman–Baron qualitative grading
- Prevention: early adequate treatment of inflammatory acne
- Atrophic: chemical reconstruction of skin scars (CROSS) with 70–100% TCA for ice-pick; subcision for rolling; punch excision/elevation/grafting for deep boxcar/ice-pick; microneedling ± PRP; fractional ablative (CO2, Er:YAG) and non-ablative (1550 nm) lasers; radiofrequency microneedling; dermal fillers (hyaluronic acid) for rolling; medium-depth peels
- Hypertrophic/keloid: intralesional triamcinolone, silicone, 5-FU, PDL, cryotherapy
- Combination approach and adequate sun protection; wait 6 months after isotretinoin for ablative procedures (traditional caution, evidence weak)

**Q11. Differential diagnosis.**
- Rosacea (no comedones, flushing, telangiectasia), perioral dermatitis, Pityrosporum folliculitis (monomorphic, itchy), drug-induced acneiform eruptions, folliculitis, milia, syringoma, adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas), steroid acne, Favre–Racouchot (comedones in sun-damaged skin of elderly), Demodex folliculitis

**Q12. Write a note on chloracne/oil acne (PYQ).**
- Oil acne: mineral oils/cutting oils in mechanics — comedones, folliculitis on thighs, forearms (where oil-soaked clothes contact)
- Chloracne: halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons (dioxins) — straw-coloured cysts and comedones on malar, retroauricular, scrotum; systemic toxicity marker; very resistant

## Quick spotter facts
- Comedones = acne (rosacea has none)
- Isotretinoin — teratogen; cheilitis universal
- Ice-pick → TCA CROSS; rolling → subcision

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Acne); Indian Acne Alliance/IADVL consensus; AAD 2024 acne guideline. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
